8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":20,"verseId":4,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Cause and Effect (Saṃbhava)","totalVerses":24,"verseData":{"id":"v20_4","number":4,"title":"If the Effect Is Not in the Cause, Causes Become Like Non-Causes","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If the effect is not in the combination Of causes and conditions, Then actual causes and conditions Would be like noncauses and nonconditions."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The consequence of non-pre-existence (v.2's horn): if the effect is INHERENTLY ABSENT from the causes, then these specific causes have no inherent connection to this specific effect. They become indistinguishable from non-causes. Why should flour (and not rocks) produce cake, if the cake is equally absent from both?","madhyamaka":"Phala sāmagrī-agata cet (if the effect isn't in the combination), hetu-pratyaya eva a-hetu-a-pratyaya-sama (causes and conditions become like non-causes and non-conditions). The absurdity: if inherent absence means NO connection, then there's no inherent reason why THESE causes produce THIS effect rather than anything else.","quantum":"Quantum specificity: even in QM, specific conditions produce specific outcomes (with specific probabilities). The double-slit experiment requires specific slits, photon source, and detector. Random objects don't produce interference patterns. Causal specificity is preserved even in quantum indeterminacy.","bridge":"Both v.4 and QM show that causes must have SPECIFIC CONNECTION to their effects — causes can't be like non-causes. QM: specific setups → specific outcomes. V.4: if effect is inherently absent, all \"causes\" are equally unconnected → absurd. Both: causal specificity requires some form of connection.","accessible":"If the cake has ZERO connection to flour, eggs, and sugar, then rocks, sand, and water should work just as well — they're equally \"not-cake.\" But they don't work. Flour specifically produces cake-like results. This specificity proves there's a connection — just not an inherent one.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: causes ARE specific — flour makes cake, not cars. This specificity is real. Ultimately: the connection is conventional (dependent designation), not inherent. Conventional specificity without inherent connection.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying all causes are equally good. Flour IS better than rocks for making cake. The verse points out that INHERENT absence (v.2) would make causes indistinguishable from non-causes — which is absurd. The absurdity proves inherent absence is wrong."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Quantum Causal Specificity — Specific Conditions, Specific Outcomes","score":55,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Even in QM, specific setups produce specific outcome probabilities. Random conditions don't. V.4: if effects are inherently absent from causes, causes become like non-causes (equally unconnected). Both: causal specificity requires some form of connection.","caveat":"Quantum causal specificity is a physics observation. V.4 is a reductio ad absurdum. The parallel is about the necessity of causal connection for causal specificity."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"Two groups: \"Causes\" (flour, eggs) and \"Non-Causes\" (rocks, sand). If the effect (cake) is equally absent from both, they become indistinguishable. Labels blur together. Absurd! Conventional specificity restored when we see the difference is conventional, not inherent.","educationalGoal":"User sees the absurdity: inherent absence makes causes = non-causes. Since causes ARE specific (conventionally), inherent absence must be wrong."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why do causes become \"like non-causes\"?","a":"If the effect is INHERENTLY absent from the causes (not connected to them in any inherent way), then the causes have no inherent advantage over non-causes in producing this effect. The cake is equally \"not in\" the flour AND \"not in\" the rocks. So why does flour produce cake? Without inherent connection, there's no inherent answer.","realLifeExample":"If a key has NO inherent connection to a lock, any key should work — they're equally unconnected. But specific keys open specific locks. The specificity proves there IS a connection (conventional, not inherent)."},{"q":"Is this a reductio ad absurdum?","a":"Yes — v.4 shows the ABSURD CONSEQUENCE of inherent non-pre-existence: causes become like non-causes (causal specificity is lost). Since causal specificity obviously exists (flour makes cake, rocks don't), the premise (inherent absence) must be false. This doesn't prove pre-existence — it shows BOTH options fail.","realLifeExample":"If \"no one is home\" (premise), then ringing any doorbell should be equally pointless (consequence). But some doorbells DO get answered (fact). So \"no one is home\" is wrong. V.4 applies this structure to causal specificity."},{"q":"How do vv.1-4 form a complete argument?","a":"V.1: effect in cause → no arising. V.2: effect not in cause → no connection. V.3: pre-existence → should be perceivable (isn't). V.4: absence → causes = non-causes (absurd). Four verses, two horns, each challenged logically (vv.1-2) and empirically/consequentially (vv.3-4). The opening section is complete.","realLifeExample":"A four-part argument against a suspect: (1) If guilty, why wasn't evidence found? (2) If innocent, why the suspicious behavior? (3) The alibi doesn't check out. (4) The alternative explanation leads to absurdity. VV.1-4 build a complete case against inherent causation."},{"q":"What is the resolution?","a":"CONVENTIONAL connection: flour produces cake not because of inherent pre-existence or inherent absence, but because of CONVENTIONAL dependent arising. The connection is real but not inherent — it's a pattern of dependent origination, not an inherent causal power.","realLifeExample":"Money buys groceries not because of inherent \"buying power\" in the paper but because of CONVENTIONAL agreement. The connection is real (money works) but not inherent (paper has no inherent value). Same for causation."},{"q":"How does this section prepare for vv.5-11?","a":"VV.1-4 showed inherent causation fails regarding SPATIAL relation (effect in/not in cause). VV.5-11 will show it fails regarding TEMPORAL relation (cause before/simultaneous/after effect). Different domain, same conclusion: inherent causation is impossible.","realLifeExample":"First proving the building is structurally unsound from the foundation (vv.1-4, spatial). Then proving it from the timing of construction (vv.5-11, temporal). Different inspections, same condemnation."},{"q":"What is the cumulative force of vv.1-4?","a":"Together, vv.1-4 establish that inherent causation fails COMPLETELY regarding the spatial relation between cause and effect. The effect can't inherently be in the cause (vv.1,3) or not in the cause (vv.2,4). Since these are the only options, inherent causation fails from the spatial angle entirely.","deeper":"VV.1-4 is a beautifully structured opening: two horns (in/not-in), each with a logical critique (vv.1-2) and an empirical/consequential critique (vv.3-4). This four-verse opening establishes the impossibility of inherent causation from the perspective of the effect's relation to the cause-combination. The rest of Ch.20 will address temporal, connectional, and essential aspects — all leading to the same conclusion. The chapter is architecturally precise: spatial (1-4) → temporal (5-11) → connectional (12-15) → essential (16-21) → conclusion (22-24)."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What happens if the effect is inherently absent from the cause?","options":["A) Nothing","B) Causes become like non-causes — there's no inherent reason why THESE causes produce THIS effect.
